8590:
Indebted means owing something to someone — either money, or a sense of deep gratitude and obligation for help you received.

Think of it this way: when someone does something meaningful for you, you feel like you "owe" them — not necessarily money, but something. That feeling, or that state of owing, is what "indebted" captures.
The Two Sides of the Word

1. The Financial Meaning (less common)

In a straightforward, literal sense, "indebted" can simply mean being in debt — owing money to a person or organization.

"The farmer was heavily indebted to the bank after taking several loans."

This just means the farmer owed the bank a lot of money. Here, "indebted" is just a more formal way of saying "in debt."

2. The Gratitude Meaning (far more common and important)

This is the meaning you will encounter most in life. When someone helps you, supports you, sacrifices for you, or does something that genuinely benefits you, you feel indebted to them. It means you feel a deep, sincere sense of gratitude and obligation — like you owe them something in return, even if you can never fully repay it.

"I am deeply indebted to my teacher, who spent hours helping me pass my exams."

This doesn't mean the student owes the teacher money. It means the teacher gave so much — time, effort, care — that the student feels a profound sense of gratitude and a feeling of being unable to fully repay that kindness.
The Emotional Weight of the Word

This is crucial: "indebted" is stronger than simply saying "thankful" or "grateful."

Here's the scale, from lightest to heaviest:

  • Thankful — You appreciate something someone did. Light and simple.
  • Grateful — You feel genuine, heartfelt appreciation. Deeper.
  • Indebted — You feel such a deep level of gratitude that you feel like you owe the person. There's almost a weight to it, like you carry an obligation because of what they did for you. This is the heaviest of the three.

So when someone says "I am indebted to you," they are saying: "What you did for me was so significant that a simple 'thank you' doesn't feel like enough. I feel I owe you more than I can ever repay."

You will very often see "indebted" paired with the word deeply:

"I am deeply indebted to you."

This is because "indebted" already carries weight, but adding "deeply" emphasizes that the feeling of gratitude and obligation is especially strong. This is one of the most natural and common ways to use the word.

The feeling of being indebted is usually triggered by something significant — not small, everyday favors. Examples:

  • A mentor who guided your entire career.
  • A friend who stood by you during a serious crisis.
  • A stranger who saved your life.
  • A parent who sacrificed their comfort for your future.
  • A colleague who defended you when no one else would.

These are acts of such weight that "thank you" feels insufficient. That gap — between what words can express and what you truly feel you owe — is exactly the emotional space where "indebted" lives.
How It Looks in Real Sentences

• "The entire village was indebted to the doctor who treated them for free during the epidemic."
  • "She felt indebted to her older sister, who had worked two jobs to pay for her education."
  • "I remain indebted to everyone who supported me during the most difficult period of my life."
  • "The country is indebted to the soldiers who sacrificed their lives for its freedom."

Notice that in all of these, the person or group has done something of real, serious significance — and the feeling of owing them goes beyond ordinary thanks.

• It does not always involve money. In most real-world usage, it has nothing to do with finances — it's about gratitude and moral obligation.
  • It does not mean you have literally signed a contract or must legally pay someone back. It's about a felt obligation, a moral and emotional one.
  • It does not mean a casual or light "thanks." If someone passes you the salt, you don't feel indebted. The word is reserved for genuine, meaningful acts.
The Big Picture — One Sentence Summary

Indebted means being in a state where you owe someone — either money in a financial sense, or, far more commonly, a deep and lasting sense of gratitude and moral obligation because of something truly meaningful they did for you.
8591:
Indecency is the quality or state of being indecent — meaning behavior, appearance, language, or content that violates accepted standards of what is proper, modest, or morally acceptable in a society, especially in relation to the body, sex, or nudity.

Think of it this way: every society has an unwritten (and sometimes written) code of what is considered appropriate in public or in shared spaces. Indecency is the act of crossing that line.

The word has two broad layers of meaning that often overlap:

1. The everyday moral/social sense

This is when someone behaves in a way that most people in a community would find offensive, shameless, or deeply inappropriate — particularly regarding the body or sexuality. It doesn't have to involve a law being broken; it's about offending a shared sense of what is decent.

  • A person who strips off their clothes in a crowded park is committing an act of indecency.
  • Explicit sexual content shown in a children's context would be described as indecency.

2. The legal sense

In many legal systems, indecency is a formal term used to describe certain sexual offences or violations of public decorum. It refers to conduct that the law specifically recognises as crossing an unacceptable boundary.

  • Public indecency refers to performing sexual acts, exposing one's genitals, or behaving in a sexually explicit way in a public place where others can see.
  • Gross indecency is a more serious legal term that historically referred to certain homosexual acts in older laws (now repealed in many countries), but more broadly it describes sexual behaviour judged to be especially serious or shocking in its offensiveness.
  • A person can be charged with indecency or convicted of indecency.

While the word can technically describe any gross violation of propriety, in modern usage it is almost always connected to one or more of these areas:

  • Nudity — particularly the unwanted or inappropriate exposure of genitals or other private parts of the body
  • Sexual behaviour — performing sexual acts where they are not appropriate, especially in public
  • Sexually explicit content — material (images, videos, writing) that is considered too graphic or offensive for a given context or audience
  • Language — occasionally, extremely crude or offensive sexual language can be called indecency, though this is a less common usage
The Role of Context and Culture

This is one of the most important things to understand about this word: what counts as indecency is not fixed. It depends on:

  • Culture — In some societies, a woman showing her hair is considered indecency. In others, topless bathing on a beach is perfectly normal and not indecency at all.
  • Time period — Standards shift across generations. Something that was considered indecency a hundred years ago may be entirely unremarkable today.
  • Setting — The same act can be indecency in one place (a public street) but completely acceptable in another (a nudist beach or an adult venue).
  • Audience — Content that is legal and acceptable for adults may be considered indecency when directed at or accessible by children.

This is why indecency is always somewhat subjective at the edges, even when the law tries to draw firm lines.

Not all indecency is equal. The word carries a spectrum:

  • Minor indecency — mildly inappropriate behaviour that offends but causes no serious harm (e.g., using crude sexual language in polite company)
  • Indecency — a clear violation, such as exposing oneself publicly
  • Gross indecency — the most serious end, involving behaviour so offensive that it is treated as a significant criminal or moral offence
How It Differs from Similar Words

• Obscenity — Obscenity is a stronger, more extreme word. It often refers specifically to content (especially pornographic material) that is considered deeply offensive and morally corrupt. All obscenity involves indecency, but not all indecency rises to the level of obscenity.
  • Vulgarity — Vulgarity is about crude, tasteless, or low-class behaviour or language. It overlaps with indecency but is broader — you can be vulgar without being sexually indecent (e.g., belching loudly at a formal dinner is vulgar but not indecent).
  • Impropriety — A gentler word for behaving in a way that doesn't fit a particular social situation. Impropriety is often used in professional or formal contexts and doesn't necessarily carry a sexual meaning.
Common Collocations (How the Word Is Typically Used)

These are the phrases you'll most often encounter with this word:

  • act of indecency — a specific instance of indecent behaviour
  • public indecency — indecency committed in a public place
  • gross indecency — the most serious form, especially in legal contexts
  • charge/conviction of indecency — legal proceedings related to indecent behaviour
  • indecency laws / laws on indecency — rules that define and prohibit indecent acts
  • standards of indecency — the threshold a society uses to judge what is indecent
  • broadcast indecency — indecent content on TV or radio

Since you're learning, it helps to see the family this word belongs to:

FormExample
Indecency (noun)The court ruled that his behaviour amounted to indecency.
Indecent (adjective)The magazine was banned for containing indecent images.
Indecently (adverb)He behaved indecently in public.
Decency (opposite noun)She expected basic decency from those around her.
Decent (opposite adjective)Wear decent clothes to the ceremony.

Indecency is the quality of behaving, appearing, or producing content in a way that violates a society's accepted standards of modesty and moral propriety — most commonly in relation to the body, nudity, or sexual behaviour — and which may be considered offensive, shameful, or, in serious cases, illegal.
8592:
To understand indecent, you first need to understand decent. Decent means behaving or appearing in a way that is acceptable, appropriate, and respectful — according to the standards that most people in a society agree on. It means not offending people's sense of what is proper, moral, or in good taste.

Indecent is simply the opposite. The prefix in- means "not." So indecent = not decent. It describes something that violates those shared standards of what is appropriate, moral, or acceptable — something that is offensive, shocking, or improper.

Meaning 1: Sexually Offensive or Morally Improper (Primary Use)

This is the most common use. Something is indecent when it involves sexual content, nudity, or suggestive behavior in a way that is considered offensive, shameless, or inappropriate — especially in public.

Examples:

  • Walking naked through a shopping mall would be considered indecent behavior.
  • A movie with extremely graphic sexual scenes might be banned for being indecent.
  • Sending someone an unwanted sexual image is indecent.

The key idea here is that the behavior crosses a line that society has drawn around what is morally and sexually appropriate. It is not just "adult" content — it is content that most people would find offensive, disturbing, or shameless.

Meaning 2: Highly Inappropriate or Lacking Respect (Broader Use)

Indecent is also used more broadly to describe something that is deeply inappropriate, disrespectful, or in shockingly bad taste — even when it has nothing to do with sex. In this sense, it means something that a reasonable, decent person would find outrageous or offensive.

Examples:

  • Laughing loudly at a funeral would be considered indecent.
  • If a powerful person offers someone money to do something corrupt or morally wrong, that could be called an indecent offer.
  • Rushing to sell your dead relative's belongings one day after their funeral could be described as indecent haste (moving so fast it shows a shocking lack of respect).
The Important Role of Society and Context

Indecent is not an absolute, fixed label. What is considered indecent depends heavily on:

  • The society or culture — What is indecent in one country may be normal in another.
  • The time period — What was indecent 100 years ago may be acceptable today, and vice versa.
  • The setting or context — A swimsuit is perfectly fine at a beach, but might be considered indecent in a courtroom.

However, the word always carries the idea that someone (often society at large, or a legal/moral authority) has decided that a line has been crossed.

These are fixed or very common combinations you will often see with indecent:

  • Indecent exposure — A legal term meaning the act of showing one's genitals in public. This is a crime in most countries.
  • Indecent assault — A legal term for a sexual attack or unwanted sexual touching.
  • Indecent haste — Moving so quickly in a situation (especially a sensitive one) that it seems disrespectful or shocking. "They buried him and sold his house with indecent haste."
  • Indecent proposal — An offer that is morally offensive, often one that involves money in exchange for something sexual or unethical.
  • Indecent behavior/conduct — A general phrase used in law and everyday language to describe actions that offend public decency.

Indecent is a serious word. It is stronger than simply saying something is "rude" or "inappropriate." It suggests a real violation of moral or social standards — something that genuinely offends a reasonable person's sense of decency. It is frequently used in legal, formal, and moral contexts.

• Obscene — Very similar, often used for sexually offensive content, but even stronger and more extreme.
  • Lewd — Focused specifically on sexual indecency; crude and sexually inappropriate.
  • Vulgar — Lacking refinement or taste; coarse and offensive.
  • Improper — Lighter than indecent; simply not appropriate for the situation.
  • Unseemly — Not fitting or appropriate, especially for the occasion; slightly old-fashioned.
  • Immodest — Showing too much of one's body, or being overly bold in a way that lacks humility.
  • Shameless — Having no sense of embarrassment about doing something wrong or inappropriate.

Key difference: Obscene and lewd are almost always about sexual content. Indecent can be sexual or general. Improper and unseemly are much softer — they suggest something is just out of place, not necessarily morally shocking.

• Decent — The direct opposite. Appropriate, proper, respectful.
  • Modest — Reserved and restrained, especially about one's body or behavior.
  • Proper — Correct and appropriate for the situation.
  • Respectable — Worthy of respect; meeting social and moral standards.
  • Seemly — Fitting and appropriate (old-fashioned).

Indecent means something that violates accepted standards of what is morally, socially, or sexually appropriate — something that most people would find offensive, shocking, or shameless. It is most commonly used for sexual or nudity-related offenses, but can also describe any behavior that is deeply disrespectful or outrageously inappropriate for the situation.
A Few Final Sentences to Lock It In

• "The magazine was banned for publishing indecent photographs."
  • "He was arrested for indecent exposure after being caught naked in the park."
  • "She was shocked by the indecent speed at which her colleagues moved on after their boss passed away."
  • "The committee found his comments about women indecent and unacceptable."

Each time you see this word, ask yourself: "What standard of decency is being violated here, and how?" That question will always lead you to the right understanding.
8593:
When something is indecipherable, it means it cannot be decoded, read, or understood — no matter how hard you try. The thing is right in front of you (you can see it, hear it, or observe it), but its meaning or content simply cannot be worked out.

Think of it this way: to decipher something means to successfully figure out what it says or means — like cracking a code, or reading a doctor's messy handwriting after staring at it for a while. When something is indecipherable, that effort fails completely. You just can't get there.
Breaking It Down Simply

The word is built from three parts:

"In" — a prefix meaning not or unable to

"Decipher" — to figure out or decode something that isn't immediately clear

"-able" — meaning capable of being done

Put them together: not able to be deciphered. That's it.
Where and How the Word Is Used

Indecipherable shows up in several real-life situations:

Handwriting — This is the most common use. If someone's handwriting is indecipherable, the letters are so messy, cramped, or carelessly written that you cannot read a single word. A doctor's scrawled prescription is the classic example people joke about.

Codes and symbols — An ancient script with no known translation key, or a heavily encrypted message with no way to crack it, can be called indecipherable. You're looking at something, but what it says is permanently locked away.

Speech — Someone's words can be indecipherable if they are mumbling severely, speaking through too much noise, or so far away that only scrambled sounds reach you.

Facial expressions and emotions — This is a more figurative use, but very common. If someone's face shows absolutely no clue about what they are thinking or feeling, their expression is indecipherable. You study their face and get nothing.

Damaged or corrupted information — A water-damaged letter, a corrupted computer file, a burned document — if the damage is severe enough that the content is completely lost, it can be described as indecipherable.
The Key Nuance: Difficulty vs. Impossibility

This is the most important thing to understand about this word.

Indecipherable does not just mean hard to understand. It means the understanding cannot happen — or has genuinely and completely failed to happen despite real effort. The barrier isn't just difficulty; it is impossibility.

Compare these two sentences:

"His handwriting is hard to read."
"His handwriting is indecipherable."

The first sentence says: with effort, you'll probably get through it. The second says: forget it — it's hopeless.

This sense of total impossibility is the emotional and intellectual punch of this word. When you call something indecipherable, you're saying, "I cannot get anything meaningful out of this, and neither can you."
What Indecipherable Does NOT Mean

It is not the same as invisible or missing. The thing exists — you can observe it — but it yields no meaning. A completely blank piece of paper is not indecipherable; it simply has nothing on it. A page filled with incomprehensible scribbles is indecipherable.

It is not the same as complicated or complex. A complicated physics equation is hard to understand, but a trained physicist can decipher it. A truly indecipherable thing resists understanding at a more fundamental level — even the most qualified person cannot crack it.
Synonyms — and How They Differ

These words are close in meaning, but not identical:

Illegible is the narrower version — it refers only to written text or handwriting that cannot be read. Every illegible thing is indecipherable, but not every indecipherable thing is illegible (a person's expression, for example, cannot be "illegible").

Unintelligible is the spoken-language cousin. It typically refers to speech or sounds that cannot be understood. "His mumbling was unintelligible" works perfectly. "Indecipherable" would also work there, but unintelligible is more natural for speech.

Incomprehensible focuses on mental understanding — something too confusing or complex to grasp intellectually. A philosophical argument might be incomprehensible, but it wouldn't usually be called indecipherable.

Cryptic means hidden, mysterious, and deliberately hard to interpret — but with cryptic, there is usually a solution lurking somewhere, waiting to be found. With indecipherable, the implication is that no solution exists or can be reached.

Obscure is much milder — it just means not widely known or not immediately clear. An obscure word is one that few people know, but a dictionary can still tell you what it means.
Antonyms

The direct opposite of indecipherable is decipherable — something that can be decoded or understood.

Other antonyms depending on context: legible (for handwriting/text), clear, readable, intelligible, comprehensible.
An Important Grammar Note

Indecipherable is what linguists call an absolute adjective — it describes a state of total impossibility, not a sliding scale. Because of this, saying "very indecipherable" or "extremely indecipherable" is logically unnecessary (like saying "very impossible"). Either something can be deciphered or it cannot.

In practice, though, you will sometimes hear "almost indecipherable" or "nearly indecipherable," and that is perfectly acceptable — it signals that something is barely understandable, right at the edge of comprehension.
Common Collocations (Words It Pairs With Naturally)

Indecipherable pairs most naturally with these words:

indecipherable handwriting / scrawl / scribble
indecipherable code / message / script
indecipherable expression / look / face
indecipherable mumbling / words
rendered indecipherable (meaning: damaged or changed to the point of being unreadable)
Register and Usage

Indecipherable sits in the range between formal and everyday language — it is educated and precise, but not stuffy. You'd comfortably find it in journalism, literature, academic writing, or an ordinary conversation between careful speakers. It is never slang, and it is never too formal to use in speech.
Putting It All Together

Imagine you find an old letter in your attic. The ink has faded, water has smeared the words, and whoever wrote it had the shakiest hand you've ever seen. You try for an hour. You hold it up to the light. You try again. You cannot read a single sentence. That letter is indecipherable.

Or imagine watching someone across a crowded room deliver what might be good news or terrible news — their face is completely flat and still, giving you absolutely nothing to read. That expression is indecipherable.

In both cases, the thing exists right in front of you — but its meaning is completely and frustratingly locked away.
8594:
Indecision is the state of not being able to make up your mind. It is the condition of being stuck — caught between two or more choices — without being able to commit to any one of them.

When someone is experiencing indecision, they have not yet decided, and the trouble is that deciding feels genuinely difficult or uncomfortable for them at that moment. It is not simply the brief pause before a quick choice. It is a state of being mentally frozen in front of a fork in the road.

"Her indecision about which job offer to accept kept her awake for weeks."
Breaking It Down Simply

Think of it this way. Imagine you are at a restaurant and the waiter is waiting for your order. You look at the menu. You go back and forth — the pasta, no wait, the pizza, but actually the salad looks good too. Minutes pass. The waiter is still standing there. You still cannot choose. That feeling of being stuck, that inability to land on a choice, is indecision.

Now scale that up to something serious — choosing a career, ending a relationship, moving to a new city — and you can feel just how heavy indecision can become.
What Makes Indecision Different from Just "Thinking"

This is an important distinction. Simply thinking before you decide is not indecision. That is just normal, healthy deliberation. Indecision is something more troubled than that. It implies:

  • That the deciding process has gone on longer than it should, or
  • That the person is genuinely unable to move forward, or
  • That the back-and-forth is causing stress, anxiety, or delay

In short, thinking is productive. Indecision is when thinking loops on itself without arriving anywhere.
The Feeling Behind It

Indecision is almost always driven by something underneath it. Common causes include:

  • Fear of making the wrong choice — "What if I regret this?"
  • Fear of losing the option not chosen — "If I pick A, I lose B forever."
  • Lack of confidence — "I don't trust my own judgment."
  • Too many options — Ironically, more choices can make deciding harder, not easier.
  • High stakes — The more important a decision feels, the harder it can be to make.

Understanding this is important because indecision is rarely about laziness. It is often about being overwhelmed, anxious, or deeply uncertain.
Degrees of Indecision

Indecision is not all-or-nothing. It exists on a scale.

  • Mild indecision: You take a little longer than usual to decide, but you get there. ("I was a bit indecisive about paint colors, but I finally chose.")
  • Moderate indecision: The decision keeps getting delayed. It becomes a source of stress. ("His indecision about the investment lasted months and cost him the opportunity.")
  • Chronic indecision: A person who habitually struggles to make decisions, even small ones, in almost every area of life. This is when indecision becomes a defining pattern of behavior, not just an occasional experience.
How It Is Used in a Sentence

Indecision is used like any regular noun — as the subject, object, or object of a preposition:

  • As subject: "Indecision is the thief of opportunity." (It steals your chances.)
  • As object: "He struggled with indecision for months before finally resigning."
  • After a preposition: "She was paralyzed by indecision." / "Out of indecision, he said nothing at all."
Words That Commonly Pair With Indecision

Certain words appear alongside "indecision" very frequently in real usage. Knowing these will help you recognize and use the word naturally:

  • Suffer from indecision — to be troubled by it
  • Paralyzed by indecision — so stuck that you cannot act at all
  • Overcome indecision — to push through it and finally decide
  • Plagued by indecision — repeatedly and persistently troubled by it
  • A moment of indecision — a brief, specific instance of being unsure
  • Chronic / constant indecision — a long-term, habitual pattern
The Tone of the Word — Is It Negative?

Almost always, yes. Indecision carries a negative or critical tone. When you call someone's state "indecision," you are implying that their inability to decide is a problem — that it is hurting them or others, causing delay, or reflecting a weakness in that moment.

It is rarely used neutrally or approvingly. You would not say "What wonderful indecision!" unless you were being sarcastic.

However — and this is a nuance worth knowing — sometimes indecision is understandable and even sympathetic. A person facing an impossible, heartbreaking choice might be described as gripped by indecision, and the reader or listener would feel compassion, not criticism. So the negativity of the word is about the state, not necessarily a judgment of the person.
Related Word Forms

Since you will encounter the same idea in different grammatical forms, here are the family members of this word:

  • Indecision (noun) — the state itself → "His indecision cost him the deal."
  • Indecisive (adjective) — describing a person or moment → "She is often indecisive." / "It was an indecisive battle — neither side won."
  • Indecisively (adverb) — describing how something is done → "He answered indecisively, never quite committing to a position."
  • Indecisiveness (noun) — very similar to indecision, but leans more toward describing it as a personal trait or quality → "Her indecisiveness frustrated her colleagues."

Quick distinction: Indecision often refers to a specific state or episode. Indecisiveness often refers to it as a character trait. In practice, they overlap heavily and are often interchangeable.
The Opposite

The direct opposite of indecision is decisiveness — the quality of making decisions quickly, confidently, and firmly. A decisive person does not linger. They weigh their options and commit. Decisiveness is generally admired; indecision is generally seen as a weakness to overcome.
One Final, Clean Summary

Indecision means the state of being unable to choose or decide. It is being stuck between options without the ability — or the will — to pick one and move forward. It is usually caused by fear, anxiety, overwhelming options, or high stakes. It is viewed negatively, as something that causes delay and missed opportunities. It can be a brief moment or a deep, chronic pattern. And it is the direct opposite of decisiveness.
8595:
Indecisive describes someone — or sometimes something — that fails to reach a clear, firm conclusion or choice. Think of it as the inability to say "yes, this one" and stick with it.

The word has two related but slightly different uses, and understanding both is key.

When you call a person indecisive, you mean they struggle to make decisions. They go back and forth between options, delay choosing, change their mind repeatedly, or avoid committing to a choice altogether — even when a decision is needed.

This is not just about taking a little extra time. An indecisive person shows a pattern of hesitation and uncertainty. They weigh options endlessly without landing anywhere firm. Even after making a choice, they often doubt it and wish they had chosen differently.

Examples:

  • "He is so indecisive that he spent forty minutes choosing between two similar pairs of shoes."
  • "She's a wonderful person, but her indecisive nature makes it hard to plan anything with her."
  • "I asked him which job offer to accept, but he just kept going around in circles — he's incredibly indecisive."

The tone of this word is mildly negative. Calling someone indecisive implies a weakness — an inability to take charge, commit, and move forward. It often suggests that the person lets opportunities slip by or frustrates others around them.
Use 2 — Describing a Situation, Result, or Outcome

Indecisive can also describe a situation, event, or result that produces no clear winner, answer, or conclusion. In this sense, it means "settling nothing."

Examples:

  • "The battle was indecisive — neither side gained any real advantage."
  • "The vote ended in an indecisive result, with no candidate winning a majority."
  • "After hours of discussion, they reached an indecisive conclusion and agreed to meet again."

Here, the word is not about a person's character — it is about an outcome that lacks a definite resolution. The situation remains open, unclear, or unresolved after it ends.

Imagine standing at a fork in the road for a very long time, looking left, then right, then left again — and still not walking in either direction. That image captures what indecisive means perfectly. There is awareness of the options, but an inability or unwillingness to commit to any one of them.

For a person, this often comes from fear — fear of making the wrong choice, fear of missing out on the other option, or fear of regret. For a result or event, it simply means the outcome did not resolve anything.

Indecisive sits at a moderate level of intensity. It is stronger than saying someone is "a bit unsure" but not as strong as saying they are "completely paralyzed." You can soften or strengthen it:

  • "slightly indecisive" — mild, occasional hesitation
  • "hopelessly indecisive" — a deep, chronic inability to decide anything

It is important not to confuse indecisive with these similar ideas:

  • Careful or thoughtful — A thoughtful person takes time to consider options wisely and does eventually reach a clear decision. An indecisive person delays and often never fully commits. Being careful is positive; being indecisive is not.
  • Open-minded — An open-minded person is willing to consider different views. An indecisive person cannot choose between them.
  • Flexible — A flexible person adjusts their decisions when circumstances genuinely change. An indecisive person changes their mind even when nothing has changed — simply out of uncertainty.

The direct opposite of indecisive is decisive — describing someone who makes clear, firm, confident decisions without unnecessary delay. Where an indecisive person hesitates, a decisive person acts. Leadership, confidence, and reliability are qualities associated with being decisive.

  • "She is incredibly decisive — she heard all the facts and made her choice within minutes."

Here are the other forms of the same word so you have the full picture:

  • Indecisiveness (noun) — the quality or state of being indecisive. "His indecisiveness cost the team valuable time."
  • Indecision (noun) — essentially the same meaning as indecisiveness, but slightly more commonly used in everyday speech. "She was paralyzed by indecision."
  • Indecisively (adverb) — in an indecisive manner. "He stared at the menu indecisively."

PersonUnable to make firm choices; hesitates, doubts, changes mind
Situation/ResultProduces no clear winner or conclusion
ToneMildly negative
OppositeDecisive

In one sentence: Indecisive means lacking the ability to make or reach a clear, firm decision — whether referring to a person's character or an outcome's clarity.
8596: Indecorous describes behavior, speech, dress, or manner that violates the unwritten rules of what is considered appropriate, dignified, or polite in a given situation. Put simply, something indecorous is socially improper — it clashes with the expected standard of conduct for a particular setting.

To truly own this word, you need to first understand decorum — because "indecorous" is simply its opposite.

Decorum is the set of standards — often unspoken — that governs how people are expected to behave, speak, and present themselves in a given context. Every situation carries its own decorum. A funeral calls for quietness, solemnity, and restraint. A job interview calls for professionalism and composure. A formal dinner calls for measured, polite conversation. When someone's behavior aligns with these expectations, they are being decorous. When they breach these expectations, they are being indecorous.
The Most Important Nuance: Social, Not Moral

This is the single most important thing to understand about this word, and many learners miss it.

Indecorous does not mean evil, wrong, or immoral. It lives entirely in the social world — the world of etiquette, propriety, and what is fitting for the moment. Laughing loudly at a funeral is indecorous. Cracking crude jokes during a formal presentation is indecorous. Wearing a swimsuit to a wedding is indecorous. None of these things are morally wicked — they are simply ill-suited to the occasion, and they disrupt the dignity or seriousness that the setting demands.

Think of it this way: morality asks, "Is this right or wrong?" Decorum asks, "Is this fitting or unfitting for this moment?" Indecorous belongs to the second question, not the first.

What counts as indecorous shifts depending on the situation. Telling a raunchy joke is indecorous at a memorial service but perfectly at home among close friends at a casual gathering. Showing up in ripped jeans is indecorous at a black-tie gala but not at a backyard barbecue. The word always implies a mismatch between behavior and setting — it is never absolute.

Indecorous is a formal word. When someone uses it, there is a sense of mild to moderate disapproval — often with an air of dignified shock or disappointment, rather than outrage. It's the kind of word a person uses when they are slightly horrified but still composed. It implies that the person behaving indecorously has embarrassed themselves, disrupted the atmosphere, or shown a lack of social awareness.

Here are several sentences to show how the word is used in practice:

  • His indecorous remarks at the board meeting left the entire room in awkward silence.
  • She was quietly asked to leave after her indecorous behavior at the ceremony.
  • Laughing during the eulogy was seen as deeply indecorous by everyone present.
  • The politician's indecorous comments, made live on air, sparked immediate backlash.
  • Arriving two hours late and making no apology was indecorous, to say the least.
  • What struck the guests as most indecorous was not what she said, but when she chose to say it.
Words Close in Meaning (and How They Differ)

Several words share territory with indecorous, but each has its own slight emphasis.

Improper is the closest and most interchangeable — it broadly means not conforming to accepted standards. Unseemly leans slightly more old-fashioned and suggests something that looks wrong or out of place in the eyes of onlookers. Unbecoming focuses on how the behavior ill-suits a person's character or position — so a judge acting unbecomingly suggests their conduct is beneath their role. Undignified zeroes in on a loss of self-respect or the appearance of seriousness. Inappropriate is the most everyday and neutral of these — it covers a wider range and lacks the formal, slightly arch flavor that indecorous carries.

Of all these, indecorous is the most formal and literary, and it carries the strongest implication that the social atmosphere has been disrupted.

Decorous is the direct opposite — meaning properly behaved, dignified, and appropriate to the setting. Seemly means fitting and appropriate in appearance. Becoming suggests behavior that suits or complements a person's position or character. Proper simply means conforming to accepted standards of behavior.

The same idea shows up in related forms you may encounter:

Indecorously is the adverb — He indecorously interrupted the speaker mid-sentence.

Indecorousness is one noun form — The indecorousness of his tone surprised everyone in the room.

Indecorum is another noun form, slightly more formal and more commonly used in writing — Such indecorum would never have been tolerated in that household.

Indecorous is a formal adjective for behavior, speech, dress, or manner that is socially improper — meaning it clashes with the expected standards of dignity, politeness, or appropriateness for a given setting. It has nothing to do with morality and everything to do with social fitness. It implies a mismatch between a person's conduct and the moment they are in, and it carries a tone of polite but clear disapproval. It is a word you will most often encounter in formal writing, literary fiction, journalism, and social commentary.
8597: "Indefatigable" is an adjective that describes a person, effort, or spirit that cannot be worn down by tiredness, difficulty, or repeated setbacks. If someone is indefatigable, they keep going with the same energy and commitment no matter how hard things get, how long something takes, or how many obstacles stand in their way. In the simplest terms, it means impossible to tire out or inexhaustibly persistent.
More than just "hardworking"

This word carries far more weight than simple words like "hardworking," "energetic," or "dedicated." Those describe effort, but indefatigable describes a kind of extraordinary, seemingly unbreakable endurance. It suggests that where most people would slow down, burn out, or give up entirely, this person does not — they just keep going with the same force and conviction as when they started.

Think of a doctor working 20-hour days in a disaster zone and still treating every patient with full care. Or a human rights lawyer who fights the same case for 30 years without losing conviction. Or a parent who tends to a seriously ill child every single day for years without ever losing their dedication. These are indefatigable people.
What kind of endurance are we talking about?

Indefatigable does not only apply to physical stamina. It can describe physical endurance (a soldier who keeps marching when others collapse), mental persistence (a scientist who keeps experimenting despite decades of failure), emotional strength (a counselor who remains fully present through thousands of painful sessions), or any combination of all three. The word is broad enough to apply to any domain where remarkable effort is sustained over time against great difficulty.
A very important nuance — it does not mean "never tired"

Indefatigable does not claim that a person literally never feels tired. Everyone feels tired. An indefatigable person gets tired too — but they don't let that stop them. The word describes the result of their character (they keep going) rather than making a biological claim about them. The tiredness simply fails to defeat them.
Always a word of admiration

This word is always, without exception, a compliment. When you call someone indefatigable, you are not just describing a fact — you are expressing genuine awe at their endurance. It carries a tone of grandeur, almost as if the person is slightly larger than life. You will never hear the word used critically or neutrally. It is never sarcastic. It is a tribute.
What can be described as indefatigable?

Most often, a person is called indefatigable — a worker, a researcher, an activist, a teacher, a volunteer. But the word can also describe qualities and efforts, such as someone's indefatigable spirit, their indefatigable campaign for justice, or the team's indefatigable rescue efforts.
How strong is this word?

It is a strong word reserved for truly extraordinary, sustained endurance — not ordinary hard work. You would not call someone indefatigable just for putting in overtime or studying late. The word is for remarkable, almost superhuman persistence, usually over a long period or through exceptional hardship. It also doesn't come in degrees the way some adjectives do — you rarely say "somewhat indefatigable." It describes an absolute quality: you either are or you aren't.
Examples in sentences

1. Marie Curie was an indefatigable scientist, continuing her research for decades despite poverty, criticism, and deteriorating health.
  2. The rescue team's indefatigable efforts over five sleepless days saved dozens of lives.
  3. He was an indefatigable advocate for the poor, never once losing his drive despite constant defeat.
  4. Even after 40 years of teaching, she remained indefatigable — as passionate about her students on her last day as she was on her first.
  5. The charity's indefatigable volunteers worked through the night to prepare meals for thousands of displaced families.
How it compares to similar words

Tireless is the closest everyday synonym and means virtually the same thing, but "indefatigable" is more formal, more literary, and carries a slightly stronger and more admiring tone. You might write "tireless worker" in a news headline; you would write "indefatigable" in a speech, a biography, or a formal tribute.

Relentless means unceasing and never letting up, but it can describe negative things too — a relentless storm, a relentless enemy. Indefatigable is always positive and always about a person or their qualities.

Tenacious means holding on tightly and refusing to let go. It focuses more on grip and determination, on not surrendering what you already have. Indefatigable is about sustained active effort going forward, not just refusing to retreat.

Diligent and hardworking are much weaker words. They describe regular, careful effort — not the remarkable, seemingly superhuman endurance that "indefatigable" implies.
When and where to use it

"Indefatigable" is a formal, literary word. You will find it in biographies, historical writing, formal speeches and tributes, quality journalism, and classic literature. It would sound strange and overly dramatic in casual conversation. In writing, however — especially when you want to pay someone a weighty, serious compliment about their endurance — it is exactly the right word.
The one-sentence summary
Indefatigable describes a level of tireless, persistent effort so extraordinary that no amount of hardship, time, or fatigue can wear it down — and it is always said with the deepest admiration.
8598:
Something that is indefeasible is so firmly and permanently established that it cannot be cancelled, taken away, defeated, or made invalid — by anyone, under any circumstances, ever. It represents an absolute, unbreakable security against any challenge.

Most things in life can be reversed. A contract can be voided. A decision can be overturned. A title can be disputed. But when something is described as indefeasible, it has crossed into a different category entirely — one where reversal is simply not possible, no matter who challenges it, no matter what argument they make, and no matter what law or authority they invoke.
The single most important distinction

"Indefeasible" is not simply a fancy word for "permanent." Plenty of things are permanent without being indefeasible. A scar is permanent, but that's not what this word means.

The word is specifically and precisely about the impossibility of legal defeat or annulment. Something is indefeasible when no process — no court, no legal claim, no rule, no authority — can undo or overcome it. The "defeat" in the word is the key. It means: this cannot be defeated.
Its opposite: defeasible

The best way to anchor this word in your mind is through its opposite. Something is defeasible when it can be cancelled or undone under certain conditions. For example, a provisional agreement might be defeasible — it can be voided if one party breaks a condition. An indefeasible right, by contrast, has no such conditions. It cannot be cancelled, period.

Think of it as a spectrum: at one end, things that can easily be undone; at the other end, things that are indefeasible — permanently immune to challenge.
Where you will encounter this word
Indefeasible lives almost entirely in formal legal, philosophical, and political writing. You will rarely, if ever, hear it in everyday conversation. These are its three main homes:
In property law — "indefeasible title"

This is by far its most common use. When someone holds an indefeasible title to a piece of land or property, it means their ownership is absolute and cannot be overthrown by any competing claim, no matter how old that claim is or how strongly it is argued.

Imagine you buy a house. Years later, someone appears and says, "My great-grandmother owned this land in 1890, and it was illegally taken from her." In ordinary circumstances, that might open a legal dispute. But if your title is indefeasible, their claim fails completely and automatically. Your ownership is locked in and cannot be touched.

This concept is especially important in land registration systems, where the goal is to give property owners complete certainty that once their title is registered, no hidden historical claim will ever come back to haunt them.
In rights and philosophy — "indefeasible rights"

Certain fundamental human rights are described as indefeasible, meaning no government, institution, or law has the authority to remove them from a person. They belong to that person unconditionally and forever.

For example, a philosopher might argue that a person's right to dignity is indefeasible — it cannot be stripped away by the state, even through legislation. It exists regardless of what any government says or does.

In political philosophy, indefeasible rights are the strongest kind of rights there are, because they carry no exceptions and permit no override.
In legal claims and interests
More broadly, a legal claim or interest is described as indefeasible when it is so thoroughly established that no rival claim can ever take priority over it or invalidate it.
What the word does NOT mean

It does not mean the physical object or thing is indestructible. A house can burn to the ground, but an indefeasible title to the land it stood on remains completely intact. The word is about legal and moral standing, not physical durability.

It also does not mean merely "very strong" or "very difficult to undo." Indefeasible means it genuinely cannot be undone. This is an absolute claim, not a matter of degree.
Example sentences

"The court confirmed that her ownership of the estate was indefeasible, and no claim from distant relatives could threaten it."

"Many moral philosophers hold that a person's right to life is indefeasible, existing beyond the reach of any government or legal system."

"Once the property title was registered under the new system, it became indefeasible — shielded permanently from any future legal dispute."

"He invested in the land only after being assured that his title was indefeasible and that no prior claim could surface to challenge it."
The tone and weight of the word

When a writer or lawyer chooses the word "indefeasible," they are making an extremely strong statement. They are not saying "this is well-protected" or "this is hard to challenge." They are saying: this is beyond challenge. This is untouchable. The word carries a sense of absolute finality — a door that has not merely been closed, but permanently sealed.
The one-sentence summary

Indefeasible describes something — most often a legal right, title, or claim — that is permanently and absolutely protected against being cancelled, overturned, or defeated by any person, law, or authority, under any circumstances whatsoever.
8599:
"Indefensible" means something is so wrong, so unreasonable, or so weak that no valid argument, excuse, or justification can rescue it. You simply cannot defend it. If you try, every attempt will fall apart.

Think of it like a court case. If someone's actions are indefensible, even the most brilliant lawyer in the world couldn't win the case for them — because the evidence, the logic, or the moral weight against it is just too overwhelming. There is no winning argument on that side.

Indefensible is used in two distinct ways, and understanding both is essential.

1. The moral and logical sense — This is by far the most common use. Something is indefensible when it is so wrong, unjust, or unreasonable that no explanation can make it okay. It goes beyond simply being "bad" — it means you cannot even construct a reasonable case for it.

A factory that deliberately dumps poison into a river used by a community for drinking water commits something indefensible. A manager who fires an employee purely out of personal hatred, with no professional reason whatsoever, makes an indefensible decision. A person who physically harms a helpless child performs an indefensible act. In each case, you could try to make excuses — but those excuses would immediately collapse under the weight of basic decency and logic. No reasonable person would accept them.

2. The military and physical sense — This is the more literal, less emotionally charged use. A place — a fort, a city, a territory, a border position — is indefensible when it physically cannot be protected from an enemy attack. It is too exposed, too open, too weak, or surrounded in a way that makes protection impossible.

A general might say: "We cannot hold this position. It is completely indefensible — the enemy can attack us from three sides, and we have no walls and no high ground." Here, the word has nothing to do with morality. It purely means: you cannot successfully defend this place. It will fall.

"Indefensible" is a powerful, uncompromising word. It does not mean "slightly wrong" or "difficult to explain." It means there is zero valid defense — not a small amount, not a weak one, but none at all.

To feel this, compare these three sentences about the same act:

"His decision was questionable." — People might debate it. Some could argue he had his reasons.

"His decision was wrong." — Most people think he made a bad call.

"His decision was indefensible." — No reasonable person can find a good argument for it. It fails completely on every level.

When you use "indefensible," you are making a firm, confident, and final judgment. You are saying: this cannot be saved by any argument, excuse, or explanation anyone could offer.
What Kinds of Things Can Be Indefensible?

Almost any noun can be described as indefensible if it fits the meaning. Some of the most natural combinations:

An indefensible act — a deed so morally wrong it cannot be justified. An indefensible position — either a stance or opinion that logic completely destroys, or a military location that cannot be protected. An indefensible decision — a choice that no good reasoning can support. An indefensible argument — a claim or case that falls apart the moment anyone examines it. An indefensible policy — a rule or law that cannot survive moral or logical scrutiny.

"The government's treatment of prisoners in that facility was widely condemned as indefensible."

"She knew her behavior had been indefensible, and she offered no excuses."

"The strategists warned that without reinforcements, their coastal position was militarily indefensible."

"He tried to explain himself for twenty minutes, but his reasons were so thin that his actions remained indefensible."

"The scientist's refusal to acknowledge the experimental data was, in the eyes of the academic community, indefensible."
How It Compares to Similar Words

Wrong simply means "not right." Indefensible goes further — it means you cannot even argue that it's right. Every attempt to argue so would fail.

Inexcusable is the closest word to indefensible and is often used interchangeably. The subtle difference: "inexcusable" tends to focus on blame and the personal failure to justify oneself — you cannot be excused, you cannot be forgiven for it. "Indefensible" focuses more on the argument itself — you cannot build a defense, a logical case, or a justification, regardless of who is trying.

Unjustifiable is also very close. It means no justification exists. "Indefensible" is slightly broader because it covers both the moral dimension and the physical/strategic dimension (as in the military sense).

Reprehensible means something deserves intense criticism and condemnation. Something can be reprehensible and still, technically, have some faint argument in its favour. Indefensible means even that faint argument does not exist.

When someone calls something "indefensible," they are making a judgment — and it is one of the strongest judgments you can make in language. The word carries the most weight and is most accurately used for things where there is a broad consensus among reasonable people: clear moral violations, logically collapsed arguments, or militarily hopeless positions.

That said, the word is sometimes used in heated debate or argument to express one person's forceful view — "Your reasoning on this is completely indefensible" — where it means: I can find no good reason for what you are saying. In that context, someone else might dispute the label. But even then, the speaker is signaling the highest level of disagreement possible: not just "I disagree" but "there is no legitimate ground for you to stand on."

The word is most honest and most powerful when the thing being described truly has no reasonable defense — and that is exactly when you should reach for it.
